The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) inquired on the orders of the day on Friday last whether or not the^e was any accuracy in the report that the enamelled post office signs that were formerly printed in blue on a white ground had been withdrawn and signs with red letters on a white ground substituted therefor. In reply to his inquiry, I wish to give the following details:
The enamel post office signs printed in blue on white background are still in use on about 11,000 post offices, and will continue to be issued to all post offices except those situated on main highways.
In 1923 the Post Office Department introduced a red enamel sign with the words "Post Office" and the name of the post office in white letters thereon, for use only on post office buildings situated on main highways only. Applications to tender on 731 of these signs were issued to eight firms and only three of these firms submitted quotations, namely, The W. F. Vilas Company, Cowansville, Quebec; the Thomas Davidson Manufacturing Company, M'Ontreal, Quebec; and the Mc-Ofaty Manufacturing Company, Montreal, Quebec.
As the tender from the W. F. Vilas Company, Cowansville, was the lowest received, the contract was awarded to that firm. This sign, which shows the words "Post Office" and the name of the post- office serves a twofold purpose:
(1)	It designates a post office.
(2)	It gives the name of the place, thus
assisting tourists.	,
Since the introduction of the sign in 1923, numerous requests ha,ve been received for the extension of its use, but the department has confined the issue to post offices situated on main traffic highways only; therefore, the blue lettered white enamel sign bearing only the words "Post Office" is still being issued to all offices not situated on main tourist traffic highways. There is no contract pending for the purchase of additional signs.

SOCKEYE SALMON FISHERIES TREATY On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this might

Sockeye Salmon Fisheries
be a convenient moment for me to make a statement regarding the government's intention with respect to the sockeye salmon fisheries convention. I notice that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has given notice of motion that the third report of the select standing committee on marine and fisheries be concurred in. That is the report which recommends that this convention should be approved by the house.
I might say that when the resolution respecting the convention was introduced it was the hope of the government that hon. members would feel that the convention was so much in the interests of this country that it would meet with approval on all sides of the house. However, as hon. members are aware, there appears to have been a considerable difference of opinion in the committee to which the convention was referred-a difference of opinion as to the ends which the treaty would attain and the motives of the government in having entered into it. Taking all circumstances into consideration, the government has thought it would be inadvisable to proceed to obtain approval of the treaty by parliament at this session.
I wish, however, to make perfectly clear the position of the government in the matter, so that there will be no possibility of misunderstanding. This treaty has been negotiated primarily in the interests of the province of British Columbia, and were it not that the opposition to the treaty has come almost exclusively from hon. gentlemen opposite who represent constituencies in that province, the government would not have hesitated one minute in proceeding with the treaty. The premier of the province has sent me the following message:
Victoria, B.C., May 30.
Press despatches intimate ratification of salmon treaty by Canada likely to be postponed consequent upon news from Washington that American senate may not consider question at present session. It is the earnest desire of this government and I am assured also that of the general public of this province that Canada should not by postponement jeopardize a work fraught with such vast potential importance to British Columbia and the Dominion. Canada having spent so many years of active endeavour in the first place to stop or restrict the destruction of this essential food asset and later to ensure measures for its restoration and protection. it would be a misfortune now that we are on the threshold of success if Canada hesitated to take the step which would complete the work so far as she is concerned. A postponement at the present time would be ground for belief that Canada is not in earnest on this question. It is urgently pressed that it be shown by prompt ratification that the dominion so far as it can do so has removed any objection in the American senate that Canada has stood aside. The government urgently request ratification at present session.
S. F. Tolmie.
What I wish to make quite clear, Mr. Speaker, is that any hesitation on the part of the government in submitting the treaty for approval at this time is in no way due to any delay in the expected ratification thereof on the part of the American senate. Mr. Tolmie says:
Press despatches intimate ratification of salmon treaty by Canada likely to be postponed consequent upon news from Washington that American senate may not consider question at present session.
Let me repeat, the action or possible action of the American senate has nothing whatever to do with our action in this matter. Indeed, we intend, if hon. gentlemen opposite from British Columbia after visiting their province between now and next session come to view the matter in a different light, as we believe they will, to reintroduce the resolution to approve this treaty early next session. In the meantime the American senate will have had an opportunity to pass upon the treaty.
I wish to make it perfectly clear that we intend to ask parliament to approve the convention next session, if in the interval it is ratified by the American senate, and we hope-that in the interim hon. gentlemen opposite-will find that the government of the province-of British Columbia-which entertains the-same view with respect to this treaty as does>
our government-is right in regard to it.

Mr. Speaker, I think the conclusion at which the right hon. gentleman has arrived is a sound one in the premises. I do not know that that will strengthen his own opinion, but at least that is my view.
The treaty in question was signed in March last, and knowledge of it came to this house some time in April. It is well that public opinion in regard to the matter should have an opportunity to crystallize. It is a treaty for sixteen years, it involves matters which most of us think of tremendous importance, and therefore the necessity is very pressing that opportunity should be afforded to those who will be affected to decide what the treaty really does mean. I think everybody will be grateful to the Prime Minister for this opportunity for public opinion to crystallize in regard to the treaty.
I may say Mr. Speaker, that so far as we who sit to your left are concerned, with respect to all matters dealing with international relations we approach them in a spirit entirely nonpolitical, or at least we endeavour to do so. It is with us not a question of Liberal or Conservative, not a question of the opposition or the government. I think we are all agreed that a satisfactory treaty is desirable. In view
31SS

Sockeye Salmon Fisheries
of the fact that the propagation of sockeye salmon takes place in the province of British Columbia and that the larger number of the salmon has heretofore been caught in American waters, it becomes of great importance that we should, if possible, arrive at some arrangement with our neighbours. A satisfactory treaty is therefore not only desirable, but is necessary for the preservation of the industry and the making available for food of this very valuable fish. But that a treaty is desirable does not make it imperative for a public man to accept as the last word any treaty that has been submitted; and there are acute divisions of opinion as to the desirability of this particular treaty. Some of the terms of the treaty are found upon analysis to be most undesirable from a national viewpoint.

I rise to a point of order.
If the hon. gentleman is to be allowed to discuss the treaty, shall I also be allowed to discuss it?

I am only endeavouring
to deal with the question raised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King); I am not going beyond that.
I ask for a ruling on the point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is well known that no debate may take place on a question arising on the orders of the day. But the right hon. the Prime Minister made a statement, and it has been always customary for the leader of the opposition to reply.
To make a statement in reply, but not a speech.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The leader of the opposition may briefly reply to the Prime Minister.
I think the rules provide in a case such as this, when the Prime Minister makes a statement, that whoever occupies the position I hold for the moment is entitled to make a statement in reply.
But not a stump speech.

The impertinence of the hon. gentleman has become so proverbial that most members in this house are unaffected by it; it is received with that disdain and contempt with which it should be treated.
I was observing that, believing as we do that a treaty is desirable and necessary, we have studied this treaty from the national point of view and find that there are acute differences of opinion with respect to some features of it. I am not aware of the views entertained by the Premier of British 
Columbia, but when I read the record it becomes quite apparent that he at least was not conversant with the terms of the treaty as it was negotiated; and the expressions of opinion he has given in the telegram that has been read make it, I think, perfectly clear that that condition has not entirely been changed. For instance, during the last twenty-four hours, I may say to the Prime Minister, one of our members has received a communication from the fishermen themselves who think that under present conditions it is not desirable to proceed with the resolution approving of the treaty. I do not desire in any sense to discuss the merits of the resolution at the moment except to observe that there are clauses in this treaty which many of us consider inimical to the national interest, and some of which at least we are uncertain as to the jurisdiction of parliament to enact or to become a party to, in view of the provisions of section 132 of the British North America Act. We are all agreed that if possible a treaty which will be fair to all parties should be negotiated between the United States and Canada, whereby those who live to the south of us may benefit from the fact that we are entirely responsible for the propagation of the sockeye salmon, while we, by reason of our less favourable geographical situation, may receive a larger proportion of the fish so propagated when they return from the sea at the end of the third or fourth year of their life. Under these circumstances I congratulate the Prime Minister upon taking the course he has, which I think is in the public interest, wholly devoid of any political consideration, and which will enable the public, by careful study and research, to ascertain fully what is involved in this treaty at this time. In that attitude we approach the solution of the problem, and not in any narrow party sense.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is one
point in my hon. friend's remarks to which I should like to refer and that is the statement that some hon. gentlemen opposite have received a communication from the fishing industry or from those interested in it, urging that the matter should not be gone on with at this stage. In the circumstances I feel I ought not to allow the attitude of the fishing industry to be in any way misrepresented so far as it is known to the government. I have received a telegram signed by Richard Gosse, representing the British Columbia Packers Limited, which is as follows:
Understand provincial government strongly pressing for ratification of Fraser River treaty this session. This request is strongly supported by entire fishing industry of British Columbia as not only does treaty give far better

Richard Gosse,
British Columbia Packers Ltd.
I think I ought to give that communication to the house as well as the one from Premier Tolmie, in order that hon. members may know that the government is fully apprised of the views of the fishing industry of British Columbia and of tlie British Columbia government with reference to this matter. I hope I have made it clear that our only purpose is not to proceed in the teeth of opposition on the part of members for the province which is mostly concerned.

The Prime Minister misunderstood me if in speaking of the fishing industry he thought I was dealing with the packing industry; I was referring to the fishermen who catch the fish. Mr. Gosse, as I know, represents the packing industry; he is,
I believe, president of the British Columbia Packers Limited. The communication received by one of my friends, who is not in the house at the moment, was from the association of fishermen-those who catch the fish. It was they to whom I referred and not the packing industry. The very terms used by Mr. Gosse. as to the government having control over the commission, involve one of the points about which great uncertainty prevails, and with respect to which we are endeavouring to ascertain what is meant. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) has just come in and has handed me the telegram signed by Mr. Maiden. It reads:
At to-day's monthly meeting fishermen opposed ratification Fraser River Sockeye Treaty this year. Am going north to-night. Send further communications regarding matter to K. Marshall.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (for Hon. Mr. Dunning, Minister of Railways) moved the third reading of Bill No. 254, respecting the construction by the Canadian National Railway Company of certain terminal facilities with grade separation and other works at and in the vicinity of the city of Montreal.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
approaches a problem of this kind with a great sense of responsibility. That sense of responsibility must necessarily follow when it is considered that a yearly fixed charge of four or five million dollars is being placed upon the country and there is a question as to whether it is to be profitable or unprofitable. In moving this amendment we have suggested that this bill should go into force through proclamation of the governor in council and after approval of the plan of the works by the Board of Railway Commissioners, but if the Prime Minister or the government of the day has some other tribunal to suggest to take the place of that body I am quite content.. I am not in any sense wedded to the Board of Railway Commissioners; my difficulty has been to secure a disinterested tribunal to which this matter could be referred.
I do not want to be considered as an alarmist, but I think that a country with a population of less than ten million and which talks as glibly as we do of expenditures of ten, twenty, forty or fifty millions of dollars, fails to appreciate and understand that obligations of this character must be met. When I say that they must be met, I mean that the interest must be paid and a sinking fund must be provided to take care of those responsibilities. Fifty million dollars is a very large obligation and a tremendous liability bo create at this time. We are talking to-day in much the same way as this country used to talk before 1914, when we had such a collapse of our railway undertakings other than the Canadian Pacific. It alarms me when I think of the way in which we cavalierly wave our hands and talk about $40,000,000 or $50,000,000 as though it were a mere bagatelle. I was content to be called a pessimist in those days, but we sowed the seed and we are reaping the whirlwind and are paying the shut to-day.
I ask, therefore, not from any political motive nor any other desire than that of making the best suggestion I can to the government of the day, that before we embark on an undertaking of this character we should pause and consider this matter very carefully. I do not make that suggestion in opposition to the terminals, because I have wondered why terminals were not long ago provided in Montreal. These facilities 'have been imperatively required by the Canadian National Railways for the last few years. The railway system must be losing money because of the inadequacy of their terminal facilities, and I have wondered just how long the Canadian people would tolerate them. But because that condition has arisen is no reason
fMr. Bennett.]
why we should not take those reasonable precautions which business men would insist upon if they were acting as a board of directors dealing with the capital of a company.
So, Mr. Speaker, without dealing with the financial features of this matter beyond what I have said, nor trespassing longer upon the time of the house, I move, seconded by Mr. Stevens:
That the bill be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole house with instructions that they have power to add thereto the following section:
"That this act shall come into force on proclamation by the governor in council and after approval of the plans of the said works by the Board of Railway Commissioners."
Any action which is to be taken should be taken promptly; there should be no delay and if the government has any tribunal to suggest which is independent and disinterested, I shall be quite content to substitute that tribunal for the Board of Railway Commissioners. I am not entirely satisfied that that board is the tribunal to which this matter should be submitted, but it is the only board of a public character of which I know to which this matter could be submitted for consideration.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the house regrets the unavoidable absence of my colleague the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) who is at present confined in the hospital. The Minister of Railways had given much time to a consideration of the various railway projects coming before the house this year. He had devoted special attention to a consideration of the different branch lines in various pants of the country, to the Hudson Bay railway extension and to the Montreal terminal facilities. He had studied these different questions very carefully. Indeed, all the members of the government know that the Minister of Railways, ever since he joined the cabinet, has been giving attention to such projects. Therefore, we regret he is not present to-day to reply to my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett).
My hon. friend, in presenting his amendment, was fair to this extent: he admits the need of new terminals and better and more economical switching facilities in the great city of Montreal, whence are shipped the products of a large part of the country. He admits that there should be no delay in carrying out the work; indeed, he says that already he is surprised that the people not only of Montreal, but of Canada, have tolerated' this

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
condition of affairs so long. I am not astonished at that, because my hon. friend, having had a good deal of experience before the railway commission and, perhaps, knowing that commission as well as or better than many others in the house, realizes the switching charges, for the moving of freight particularly, in Montreal, are very high and he knows that it is the man back home who pays those switching charges. But, having made that statement as to the imperative necessity of the work, my hon. friend suggests that before going on with it, we should refer it to a board in which he frankly tells us that he has not as much confidence as he would like to have. I repeat that he is in a position to know, because he has appeared before the railway commission many times.

Not as it is at present
constituted'.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What does my hon. friend
mean by that?
I mean that it is not the board it once was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is another admission
that my hon. friend is asking us to refer the consideration of this great problem to a board in which he himself has-I will not say no confidence, but little confidence. This project of the Montreal terminals is, so far as the railway is concerned, not a matter of hasty conclusions. The Canadian National railway management have been considering this problem for more than six years. Not only have they been looking into it very carefully through their own engineers, but they have brought to Canada an independent engineer, a recognized and most capable terminal engineer, who has had experience not only in the mother country but in other parts of the world. I understand they have had the advantage of the experience of eminent railway engineers connected with other vast railway transportation systems on this continent. They have examined carefully the terminal facilities in other cities and after all this examination and study have reached the conclusion that the plan now presented to parliament is one that will take care of the necessities of the great port of Montreal not only for the immediate present but for years to eoime.
What does this terminal plan as presented accomplish? It solves three problems. It solves the grade problem, the crossing problem of the different grades. Everyone admits that with the congested condition now existing
in our cities, that is important, and eighty-one grade crossings are taken care of by this readjustment. Is it not important that that work should be proceeded with without delay? It also takes care of the readjustment and coordination of the present transportation facilities and reduces to a considerable extent the cost of switching. It provides for a belt line for freight and passengers right around the city of Montreal-and also, unlike the situation that exists in other railway stations in Montreal, where the lines come to dead ends, it provides for a continuation of the system through the city, so that trains coming from the wrest proceed through to the east and trains coming from the east are able to proceed west. It is not proposed to spend this $51,000,000 immediately because the bill specifically states that the management may take seven years to do the work. I imagine that the people of Montreal and, indeed, the people of all Canada will want this work completed as soon as possible.

The bill provides for a
period of five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thought it was seven. The
expenditure covering that period of five years, as stated by my hon. friend, is not unreasonable. In the bill before parliament, the same precautions are taken in regard to the Montreal teiimimails as were taken in connection with the various branch line bills that parliament has passed. It is subject to the same examination and conforms in every respect to the general Railway Act.
As regards the expenditure, I take issue at once with the leader of the opposition. The people of Canada are not disposed to be governed by commissions. The government of the day are responsible for the spending of the people's money. If the people of Canada decide that the government are unwisely spending the public money, we shall be put out of office and my hon. friend will be put in. But the people will have an opportunity to judge us. Will they have such an opportunity if we turn over to the Board of Railway Commissioners, a board in which my hon. friend has just said he has little confidence, the decision as to whether or not the Canadian National railway management is going to spend this $50,000,000 or $51,000,000? If we do so, what chance have the taxpayers of Canada to turn them out if they are not satisfied with them? So I say to my friend that it is better that a government responsible to the people should be charged with the responsibility of making this decision. Even assuming that we adopt the suggestion of my

C.N.K.-Montreal Terminal
hon. friend and refer those plans to another board for consideration, how is that other board going to secure the desired information? Have we no confidence in the management of the Canadian National Railways? If we have no confidence in them, the proper amendment to bring in would be that we change the situation and turn over the management of the railway to the Board of Railway Commissioners.

My hon. friend is a
business man. Did he ever know of a business man who was engaging in large capital expenditures not calling in experts for their opinions, while at- the same time not dispensing with the reports of his own managers and engineers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend has just told us that he questions whether the Board of Railway Commissioners are experts. The Canadian National railway board, through its chairman and directors, responsible to the people through the government of Canada, have not brought this measure to parliament without first taking expert advice. They have not come here hastily, for they have been considering this project for six years. Is it necessary that I should repeat to my hon. friend that they have obtained the advice of an independent expert terminal engineer? They brought to this country Mr. Palmer, who is regarded as one of the best railway terminal engineers in the old world.
There is another railway terminal engineer whose opinion has also been given in favour of this project, a man in whom the country had some confidence a few years ago, and in whom I believe they have confidence yet. I remember that when the government was looking about for a suitable man to take charge of this great national railway system that we had on our hands, there was some criticism of the selection of Sir Henry Thornton. It was recognized that he was an excellent railway terminal engineer and that he had had great experience in providing terminal facilities for railways in large cities, but some questioned very much whether he was a good traffic manager. They said they were not very sure as to that. We know, they said, that the government have selected a good railway terminal engineer, but we are not sure that he is a good traffic manager.
Who said that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend recalls that that was the criticism at that time.

I am frank to say that I never heard it.
[Mr. Robb.)

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I leave it to the Canadian people to decide whether or not Sir Henry Thornton has proven himself a good traffic manager. I submit that if Sir Henry Thornton was a good railway terminal engineer when he was engaged as president and chairman of the board of directors of the Canadian National railway, he has not lost anything by the experience of the past six years and by the exchange of opinions that he has had with other eminent railway engineers.
We entrust to the chairman and board of directors of the Canadian National railway, which is owned by the people of Canada, the expenditure of about $245,000,000 every year, and no one has suggested that before the management spend part of this money they should consult the Board of Railway Commissioners, a board in whioh my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has but doubtful confidence. If the chairman and the board of directors of the Canadian National railway are to be entrusted with the building of branch lines throughout the country, with the extension of the Hudson Bay railway, and the operation of the vessels that we have on the ocean, surely they are to be entrusted with the expenditure of the money that parliament is voting for the Montreal railway terminals.
I repeat again that it is the government of the day that is responsible. The government must pass on all this expenditure and the government would not pass on any of this expenditure unless it was satisfied, as it is satisfied now after examination, that the railway has obtained the best expert engineering advice and that the terminals proposed are suitable to the requirements of the great port and city of Montreal. The bill provides that the expenditure shall not be more than $10,000,000 in any one year. I repeat that it is the governor in council that must authorize the expenditure of this money. The government of the day is responsible and so I ask parliament, admitting with my hon. friend that there is necessity and immediate necessity for improved railway terminal facilities in Montreal, why we should delay the passing of this measure by referring it to a board in which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has just said that he has but little confidence.
Mr. C. II. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):	Mr. Speaker, I am speaking entirely unexpectedly because I had no knowledge that this amendment w-ould be proposed to-day. The greater part of this work will be carried on in the constituency which I have

C.N.R.-Montreal Terminal
the honour to represent in the city of Montreal. I have taken particular pains during the last fortnight to ascertain what the general public opinion is in Montreal with regard to the extension of these terminal facilities. Montreal, it is impossible to disguise the fact, is proud of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has brought great credit to the city of Montreal during the last fifty years, and Montreal has always had faith and confidence m the management of that great undertaking. Public opinion, as I understand' it, in the city of Montreal is most desirous that there should be a clear and amicable understanding between the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways with regard to terminal facilities; but apparently up to the present time the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is not prepared to enter into a joint undertaking for the construction of terminal facilities, believing, as is undoubtedly the fact, that its present terminal facilities and the splendid station and equipment, which it now has, will be quite adequate to the requirements of its own undertaking for a number of years to come, and therefore public opinion, as I understand it. is that the way should be left open, as the development of the terminal facilities of the Canadian National Railways proceeds, for an amicable understanding, if one may be reached, by which the Canadian Pacific Railway may come in and share in those facilities. The door should be left open.
Apart from that, public opinion in the city of Montreal, as I understand it, is so thoroughly dissatisfied with the present terminal facilities of the Canadian National Railways in that city that, so far as it may give expression to the public opinion of this country, so far as it can exercise any influence on the government of this country, it will insist that there shall be no delay in proceeding to remedy the existing distressing and deplorable conditions. Therefore, representing that city, it is necessary, I think, for me to say that the general opinion of the city as a whole is that the work should proceed rapidly and that there should be no unnecessary delay in its commencement.
I have 'been accustomed to examining engineering plans for a number of years, and I am thoroughly convinced that so far as the engineering problems are concerned, there are no great engineering difficulties to be overcome in carrying out the undertaking for the proposed construction of these terminal facilities in the city of Montreal. So far as construction is concerned, I have no doubt that, there will be no difficulty in finding not only

I desire to inquire of the
Acting Minister of Railways (Mr. Robb), as I would have inquired of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning)

whose absence I in common with all other members of the house deeply deplore-if any steips have been taken by the government to remedy the situation which has arisen in Quebec, a situation created by the application of the Maritime Freight Rates Act to the city of Quebec and the surrounding country. It would appear that owing to that legislation the city and port of Quebec have been seriously discriminated against. The Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General and members from the district of Quebec have received memorials in protest, and it has been quite conclusively shown to the Minister of Railways and others that owing to the application of this legislation the harbour of Quebec is, so to speak, divided- into two: freight shipped from Levis, which is in the harbour boundaries of Quebec, obtains considerable advantage over freight shipped from the city of Quebec, so much so that at the present time the merchants of the city of Quebec meet competition from the maritime provinces almost at their door. Within 50 or 60 miles of the city of Quebec the freight rates are on a par with those from Halifax; whereas the merchants of Levis have received benefits which even they did not anticipate.
I submit that this was on oversight at the time the legislation was passed. For many years Quebec and Levis were in the same rate zone. Serious injury has been occasioned bo the merchants and the shippers of the city of Quebec, and they have protested vigorously. They have taken their protests to the proper authorities here. Moreover, they went down to the maritime provinces and explained their case to the boards of trade of Halifax and St. John. Not having anticipated that this matter would come up for discussion this afternoon, I have not the documents at hand which I should have, but I believe their representations received not only a sympathetic hearing, but I am under the impression that resolutions of these boards of trade were

If he will join with me and other members from the maritime.?; to have the Maritime Freight Rates Act extended to Montreal, I am with him.

In reply to the unselfish
remarks of my hon. friend, I ^hall be glad to join with him in any way-

Then start on the right
track.

I never claimed, nor did
anybody else in the city of Quebec, that the Maritime Freight Rates Act was intended for our relief; but I did wish to make it clear that that legislation was not intended unjustly to discriminate against the port and city of Quebec. The effect of the introduction of those rates has been to deprive the merchants of Quebec of the opportunity to sell their goods in territory which from the earliest days has been recognized as their own. Anyone who is familiar with the geographical situation of the province of Quebec will know that almost all the territory between Montreal and Three Rivers on both the north and the south shore of the St. Lawrence river is fully covered by the business people of Montreal; whereas the territory below the city of Quebec, between it and the New Brunswick border, has been for years that in which the Quebec merchants were able to carry on their business.

You
are referring to the city of Quebec?
Yes. The effect of these rates is that we are no longer able to carry on business there.

Will the hon. member go
ahead! and prove his proposition? I am sympathetic, but I should like to hear from him something more than a mere assertion.

My hon. friend's point is
absolutely well taken. Unfortunately I did not expect this matter to be brought up to-

day and I have not with me the memorial of the Quebec board of trade. It is quite clearly stated that on certain articles the rate from Quebec to Ste. Anne de la Pooatiere, eighty miles below Quebec, is about equal to that from St. John to the same point, which is about four hundred miles. I do not remember all the details, but if that is the case, and if it can be shown, then there is an unjust discrimination. No favouritism should be shown in that territory. That is the point, and it should be the duty of the government to make a more serious investigation into the matter than has so far been made.

I am glad the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has brought this matter to the attention of the committee. I for one, as a member from Quebec, have had occasion more than once to meet representatives of the various commercial interests of that city with a view to bringing to the attention of the government the discrimination under tvhich the city of Quebec is labouring by reason of the freight rates consequent upon the Duncan report and the act based thereon. As stated by the hon. member, it is well known that the city of Quebec has always been regarded as a part of the maritime provinces so far as traffic is concerned. Everyone who has spent a few years in Quebec will remember the time when we had a ferry which often carried full trains across from Levis to Quebec and from Quebec to Levis, in the traffic between the maritime provinces and that city. Knowing all the circumstances, and being under no doubt at all as to the city of Quebec having been all along regarded as a part of the maritime provinces in the matter of freight rates, we were very much surprised to learn that in the Duncan report only the city of Levis was mentioned; and no one -at the time protested, for the simple reason that it was inconceivable to the people of Quebec that the mention of the word Levis alone could be taken to mean anything else than the inclusion of Quebec city itself. The city of Levis is, of course, a splendid place but it is not to be compared in importance to the city of Quebec; everyone will concede that. It is well known that our commercial people have long done business with the maritime provinces, carrying on a considerable trade with them. When the word Quebec was omitted from the timetable the officials of the department and of the -railways concluded that the special freight rates did not apply to that city. It is then that the question began to attract attention, and as soon as the discrimination was realized the members representing that city, the -board -of trade and the

Supply-R ailways-C .N.R.
various interests of Quebec took action to bring the matter to the notice of the government. I may say that so far we have received a very sympathetic hearing, but that is about all that we have obtained. I am glad that the members from the maritime provinces appear to be in sympathy with our claim in this matter, and I sincerely trust that as a result of these combined efforts the government will see its way clear to giving the city of Quebec the freight rates which the maritime provinces enjoy under present conditions.

It may be true, and I think it is, that we are sympathetic with the desires of the people of the city of Quebec, but I cannot say that we are sympathetic to the point of wishing them to get what they ask for in this particular case. The minister will no doubt give due consideration to all the representations submitted to parliament, but he will find that there is a very strong and widespread objection to this application from the city of Quebec. There is one way that is suggested of helping to meet the situation and that is, instead of having the point fixed at Levis, that it be extended back some miles to St. Charles or some station nearer the maritime provinces. In that way there might be eliminated any difficulty arising between Levis and Quebec. In the meantime, while we wish our friends in Quebec every consideration, we do not propose that anything shall be done which will interfere with the Maritime Freight Rates Act as passed by parliament. There may be some way by which to meet the situation so far as Quebec is concerned without disturbing the maritime rates. But what is proposed just now by hon. members from Quebec we consider to be very injurious to the act which gives us the 20 per cent reduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I assure my hon. friend that the matter has been submitted to the various maritime boards of trade and as recently as last week ten of them out of twelve had approved of the demand made by Quebec in this respect. It is really as much in the interests of the maritime provinces as of Quebec itself that this request is being made. As the hon. member for Quebec South had said, it seems anomalous that part of Quebec harbour should be subject to the preferential rate while the other part of the harbour is not. May I say-and I am surprised that my hon. friend from Quebec South forgot to say it-that when the delegation came to submit this request the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) recognized that the grievance existed, stating that the officers of the department would try to find a means
of remedying it, perhaps without the necessity of having recourse to legislation. But he added that if legislation were necessary it would be considered prior to the next session of parliament. I may tell my hon. friend that we are far from trying to hurt or in any way impair the charter which has been given the maritime provinces; far from it. The demand made by Quebec, if opposed by those interested in maritime matters, such as the boards of trade, would not be entertained, I am quite sure. But it is with the consent and the approval of our friends from the maritime provinces that the subject has been brought to the attention of the government.

If the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will carefully and judicially read the resolution prepared by the maritime boards of trade, I do not think he will be able to put upon it the interpretation which he has now given to the house.

I have heard of the representations which have been made but I have not had an opportunity to listen to them directly nor have I been able to consider them fully. I feel, however, that the hon. member for Quebec South ought to accept the assurance that these representations will be considered. Speaking for myself, I do not feel that I should bind myself, or consider myself bound by these representations until all sides have been heard and everyone who is interested has had a chance to present his case. I am not sure that it is enough that the Quebec representatives have waited upon the maritime boards of trade and discussed the matter with them. Until the views on all sides have been formally put on record and considered, I think judgment should be reserved. In my opinion, the present moment is not opportune to make a declaration; we should wait until everyone has had an opportunity to present the matter. I am not sure that there is a clear view in the maritime provinces as to just what is implied in regard to the question of implementing the Duncan report or carrying out the principle contained therein with regard to special provision for freight rates.
Nor is there a general consent of the boards of trade. I think the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) will agree to that.

As one of the representatives of the section of Quebec which might be affected by the matter brought up by the hon. member for Quebec South, I may say that this matter offers first of all
Supply-Railways-C.N.R.

some local difficulties as between the people of Quebec and the people of Levis, which must toe settled, and other difficulties as between the people of Quebec and the people of the maritime provinces which also must be adjusted. This is a matter which certainly cannot be settled by simply bringing it up in this house arid asking the government immediately to bring about a settlement. Only recently the government has been called upon to give its attention to this matter; the Minister of Railways received a delegation; the board of trade of the city of Quebec is now in touch with the boards of trade of the maritime provinces, and I have no doubt that everyone interested will be satisfied when it is stated that the government is giving the matter serious attention. Pending the outcome of the negotiations now going on between the different commercial interests it would be useless for us in this House of Commons to attempt to bring about a settlement. This is a matter which will have to be examined very carefully and I have no doubt that in conjunction with our friends from the maritime provinces, next year we might be in a position to reach a satisfactory adjustment.

I am afraid I must take issue with the Solicitor General as to the date at which this matter was brought to the attention of the government. It is all very well for my hon. friend to say that this is an occurrence of only recent date, but after all four months surely is a sufficiently long time even for this government. The Solicitor General and the Minister of Justice will recollect that shortly before the beginning of this session they were interviewed in Quebec by a delegation from the board of trade and by the members for the Quebec district, and when the necessity and urgency of the matter was presented to them they said they would take action as soon as it was convenient to do so.

And they recommended to our Quebec friends that they get in touch with our friends from the maritimes and try to reach a settlement, and that is what is going on now. I do not think we are helping to bring about a settlement by this present discussion.

I am not prepared to agree with my friend the Solicitor General; I am one of those who believe with President Wilson in the principles of open covenants, openly arrived at. I would much prefer to discuss this matter fairly and openly on the floor of the house with my hon. friends from

the maritimes in order that we may be able to come to some settlement. Had we continued to agitate in the Quebec papers I am afraid those papers would have been read by very few of the hon. gentlemen opposite; some of them would not be able to read those papers, so I thought it beet to bring the matter before the members of the house in this way as we brought it to the attention of the members of the government four months ago and again one month ago, at which time we were told that our request was receiving the consideration and sympathy of the government.	[DOT]
Serious consideration.

Yes, serious consideration. Now I suggest that we might be told that some steps are being taken, at any rate, to put an end to this situation, and it is not sufficient to tell us that because the hon. member for Quebec South rises in his place and draws the attention of the house to a matter affecting his constituency and his city he is probably disrupting certain negotiations of which he at any rate knows nothing. If I had been informed that negotiations were going on or that the work was progressing favourably possibly I might have been able to return to my constituents and tell them to be patient a little longer, but they are tired of being patient and they would like to have some assurance from the government that their claims will be dealt with.
I wonder if I caught the language of the Minister of Justice correctly; sometimes I do not hear very well, but I thought I heard him mutter the words, "Et tu Brute."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg your pardon; was my hon. friend asking me something?
I was asking the Minister of Justice if I was right in thinking I heard him say, " Et tu Brute."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, that is a language I do not usually use.

It is rather amusing to find some of our friends from Quebec apparently now of the opinion that the Maritime Freight Rates Act was passed for the benefit of the central provinces. My understanding is that the Maritime Freight Rates Act arose out of a recommendation of the Duncan commission, which pointed out that we in the maritimes were handicapped by 2o0 miles of railway built or diverted for strategic purposes, and to overcome that extra mileage we were to be given a preferred rate.

Supply-National Defence
My contention is that when the western point to which those rates should apply was determined that was not done fairly; that point should have been Montreal, because as I stated before, Montreal is the gateway through which we can or must distribute our products throughout the central and -western provinces, since we have practically no trade east of Montreal. I have not the slightest objection to getting into Quebec on the same terms, but our trade with the city of Quebec and that part of the province of Quebec east of Montreal is comparatively slight. At Montreal we practically encounter the inflow from the foreign markets of Great Britain, Belgium, Germany and Europe generally and there we also meet the Ontario producers of iron and steel who ship by water. Unless we can get fair rates to the city of Montreal we will derive very little benefit from the Maritime Freight Rates Act. We are interested not at all in the traffic going east; that is not the important matter. What we are interested in is the opportunity to get into the markets of these central provinces; the eastern traffic affects us very little. I am content that we should pay any reasonable rates as far as the trade going east is concerned, but we must have an opportunity to get into the central markets.

I can hardly be under any misapprehension as to the purpose of the Maritime Freight Rates Act; for two or three years we heard nothing but appeals from the maritime members for relief and justice. I may say, however, that the members from Quebec never opposed this legislation on that ground; on the contrary, all the members from Quebec were only too glad to help relieve the maritime situation in every possible way. We were quite willing to be of assistance to the maritimes; we were glad to help them in any way, but I do not think we should be called upon to ruin ourselves for the sake of helping our neighbours. That is the position.

Item agreed to.
Department of National Defence-militia services-administration, $317,000.
What explanation has the minister to offer for the general increase in the militia estimates over last year, particularly in view of the fact that this year the Paris pact was signed?

This is a Liberal
government.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
I do not think the question is
quite justified by the estimates as they appear on page 26 of the main estimates. My hon. friend will see that there is no increase in the military estimates. There is an increase in connection with the naval vote, and there is another increase in connection with civil air operations. The increase in the naval estimates is brought about by the purchase of two destroyers to replace the Patriot and the Patrician which, it will be remembered, were presented to Canada in 1920 by the British government along with the cruiser Aurora. Although this item appears to be increased this year I would point out that in fact it is not an increase over last year. There was an increase last year of $900,000 to take care of the first payment on account of these two destroyers, but this amount was not used. Had it been used the vote this year would have been the same as it was last year, but in view of the fact that it was not used it was necessary to revote that amount plus the amount of the second instalment which will be due this year.
I have the details of the civil air operations if they are desired by my hon. friend, but I can assure her that they are not military in any sense of the word but are connected with the increased service which the civil government branch of the department is providing, particularly for the Department of the Interior.
If they are not military in character why do they come under the Department of National Defence?

As my hon. friend knows, that is a matter of organization. The air board which was formed some years ago was put under the Department of National Defence, and it h^s remained there. In view of the representations which were made two years ago it was thought advisable to divorce completely the civil government operations from the so-called military operations-I will explain that when we reach the particular items-and a distinct civil government branch was formed. This branch is in the same position as other administering services which perhaps have nothing to do with the particular name of the department.

Are the civil pilots trained
by the military personnel?

The camp at Borden
trains civil pilots, as well as military pilots. It may be some relief to some of the members of the committee, whose views I know very
Supply-National Defence

well, to learn that in view of the increase in civil aviation and in the demands made, not only for the government services but to assist in connection with aviation in Canada, that the camp at Borden is being used principally as a training ground for civilian work. Perhaps that may be regarded with something of a shock by some members of the committee who may feel that we are going back on military training, but it was felt that the training which we could give at Camp Borden was necessary and essential for the promotion of civil aviation in this country where aviation is so beneficial.

Are the pilots technically
trained at Camp Borden?

We require that those
accepted for training shall have undergone a c-ourse of applied science at some university. This technical training is being given by universities throughout the country. We do not take a man in off the street, so to speak, and try to make a pilot out of him; we ask that he have some preliminary training. We have neither the force nor the facilities to conduct an elementary school, and therefore the student must have already the theoretical training before he is admitted. We believe that the success of aviation depends very largely upon the safety with which it can be carried on, and safety, after all, is made up of ground organization as well as the actual flying ability.

Is there any lack of men
applying for training in the civil air service?

There is no lack of men
applying, but I must say that none too many meet	our	qualifications. In	that	regard, Iwould	say	to the committee	that	a numberof provisional pilot officers were required this year.	We	circularized the flying	clubs andschools but we have not been able to find the required number of partially trained men. I do not intend that as an invitation to members of the committee to recommend various gentlemen.	We	have been very	careful in our
selections, believing, as I said a moment ago, that the very foundation of aviation in this country requires that the men be thoroughly trained.

Instruction is being carried
on at various places and one hears of many bad accidents where a lad, probably on his first solo flight, has crashed. At times these men have been seriously injured, and at other times the crash has resulted in death. I do not say for a moment that that is brought

about through insufficient training or anything of that sort, but I would Like to ask the minister what steps are being taken to make certain that there is that degree of instruction received and ability shown before the men are given a flying license.

Without casting any
reflections upon the organizations, I think the accidents to which my hon. friend refers have occurred mainly in flying clubs, especially those occurring this year. The service this year has been singularly free from accidents, although we had one bad accident last year in the west. These flying clubs are purely civilian organizations and the department assumes no responsibility for their maintenance, upkeep or supervision except that which would be taken in connection with a commercial organization such as, for instance, the Western Canada Airways. The department requires that the pilots shall pass our tests, and they are medically examined every six months. The machines are inspected before a license is issued, and are inspected each year before the new license is given out. In addition to that we are constantly in touch with these clubs. In connection with the accident which occurred the other day, while the department was under no obligation we immediately conducted an inquiry in an endeavour to find out the cause of the accident in order that we might take steps to prevent a recurrence of such an accident. Where lack of judgment has been shown or anything else brought to light which would indicate that something was wrong with the machine, we immediately advise these clubs to that effect. These flying clubs are generally managed by groups of enthusiastic men who are keen on aviation, and we are always afraid that familiarit}' will breed contempt. WTe are endeavouring to get them to see that what I said a minute ago is absolutely essential, namely, ground organization. That means inspection every morning of the machines and every part which may be frail or give way; that they must observe regulations which we lay down in regard to these flying clubs; that the instructors must be passed as medically fit, because in no branch of activity in Canada is it so necessary that men shall be medically fit and that certain disabilities shall be absent as it is in connection with flying.

Does the department give
any supervision to these flying clubs and the instructors to see that the proper training is given?

The general answer is
no; that is to say, except to examine the instructors whom the flying clubs use and

Supply-National
Defence
see that they are licensed pilots and pass our regulations. We examine the machines and see that they comply with the necessities for a license. Then we examine the so-called pupils to see whether they are fit to receive either a private or a commercial license as the case may be.

What is the usual length of
time for an applicant to receive his certificate under the department's training?

Fifty flying hours for a
commercial pilot and ten flying hours for a private license. A private license means that one cannot carry passengers.
But how long does he usually have to spend at the training course in order to secure that certificate-six months or a year?

Anything from a month
up. It depends upon the man. As regards our own pilots, these young pilot officers whom we are training, they spend three vacations, sometimes four. That is to say, in order to get their full training for both ground instruction and flying, they have to spend a year or so. For the pupils in the flying clubs a month would be the very minimum, but the course usually takes a great deal longer than that. A man will 'be in the air for perhaps a few minutes only the first day, and I think from a month to six months would be the minimum.

I should like to know
whether non-commissioned officers and men disabled in the air service receive a pension, whether in case of their being killed, their dependents receive a pension, and if so, how much.

I think I furnished my
hon. friend with information along that line last year. I do not have it in my mind at the minute, because it involves amounts and regulations, but I shall be glad to give the information before the committee rises. Is my hon. friend dealing with the members of the department? Of course, my hon. friend knows that no pensions are paid in respect of those who are pupils in flying clubs.

I have tried to get the information from the regulations and have absolutely failed. Perhaps the minister could tell me in a general way whether the noncommissioned officers and men in his department who are engaged in flying, receive a pension in case of disability or death.
In a general way I may say yes, they do.

I think there are some
peculiarities about this.

If there are any jokers
and if my hon. friend will point them out, I shall be glad to see that they are remedied.

I cannot find any jokers
because they are so wrapped up in the regulations.

If my hon. friend knows
of any case where there has been some reservation or condition and if he will bring it to my attention, I will take it up at once. If men are hurt while they are engaged in the service, it is the intention that they shall be pensioned.

I was not in the chamber
when this item was brought up and perhaps the minister has already replied to the question I am going to propound. In view of the great number of young Canadians^ who are very anxious to enter the Royal Air Force,
I should like to know what are the essential educational qualifications.

Speaking of the position
of a pilot officer, let me say that generally the educational qualifications required ar& graduation from a university or from the Royal Military College, or that a man is actually attending a class in applied science at a recognized university and undertakes to finish his course in that respect. Hon. members will understand that applied science, physics, dynamics and aeronautics, is essential in connection with the care and handling of the machine. If such an undertaking is given, the applicant will be considered for training, as I indicated a little while ago, during his vacation for the three or four years that he is attending a university. Therefore the issuing of his pilot's license will probably be coincident with his graduation from the university.
In connection with airmen, that is, those who are not pilot officers, we do not insist on educational qualifications. We have no definite standard. We would like them to have matriculation qualifications, but what we insist on is either that they shall be students at a technical college for two or three years or that they shall have worked for, say a year or two in connection with gas engines and machinery of that sort. Many of our airmen are mechanics, men who have been connected with garages, who have had to do with automobile engines for a substantial period of time. We do not take a man off the street, for instance, out of a grocery store, and make him an airman, because we have not the facilities nor the personnel for giving him elementary training.

As this is a very important question and as I said, so many young Canadians are ambitious to enter the Royal Air Force of Canada, it is evident from what the minister has said that nothing is definitely stated regarding the qualifications, say of cadets. As regards age, boys of eighteen years are ambitious to enter the Royal Air Force. What is the minimum age at which a young Canadian is allowed to enter that force? If there is any rule I should like to know it, because I know many young men to-day who have matriculated from the various high schools into the different universities and who are now engaged, just as my hon. friend has said, in grocery stores and other lines of business, but who are not engaged in what we call technical industries. I would like to have that point cleared up because I have on my file over sixteen letters of inquiry regarding it, and when the minister gives me the information I shall be able to inform my correspondents.

He must :be over the age of eighteen years and under the age of twenty-one when he commences his course. The case to which my hon. friend refers I understand1 *is that of a university graduate in applied science who has gone into some other vocation. If he is physically fit, is within the age limit and complies with all the other requirements, he would be eligible for consideration.
Thank you.

I have a complaint to make in regard to the civil air operations. Perhaps it does not come under this vote, but if the minister will give me the information I can report back later. A young man named Keeley in my constituency entered for a course of civil air training. At that time the department recognized these commercial companies which had been formed for the training of aviators for commercial flying. The young man entered the service of a company which was recommended by the department. That company very soon afterwards became bankrupt, and the young man then entered two or three other companies, but for one reason or another his training was deferred. Finally he came to the stage when he was to make his solo test flights. Everything had been satisfactory up to that time. He had been examined by medical officers and had been seen by the officer in charge, but when he came to take his solo trial flights it was found that he had one defect, that he was wearing glasses. I am not going to justify the acceptance for the service of any man with a defect, but it does appear to me that some person up to that time should have

noticed that he .was wearing glasses. He had taken this course with the intention of receiving a certificate for commercial flying and his people had spent $2,000 on his training, but after the expenditure of that amount and the failure of two or three of these guaranteed commercial companies, it was ruled that he could not take his solo test flights because he was wearing glasses. I am behind the department's examination. I have seen it, and I think the requirements are pretty nearly perfect, but I do think that in this case someone made a mistake, and that this young man should not have been allowed to go on with his training to the point where it has now become burdensome to his people, if he is not to be granted a certificate. He entered the service of one company after another and had passed every test up to the time of his solo flights. He had made a landing or two perfectly. The minister kindly took the matter up and said that he would give him a certificate, but it would not be a commercial certificate. Of course that is what the young man was training for, and that is what his people spent the $2,000 for. But through a defect which some person should have noticed this young man is not allowed to take his final tests, although he could really qualify, and he cannot in consequence get his certificate.

My hon. friend is quite
right in saying that he brought the matter to my personal attention some time ago and1 I was trying to get into my head as he was speaking the exact facts. As I remember it, this student was examined by outside medical men, I think, on two different occasions.

If the minister
will remember, these two men who examined him were the department's own accepted examiners.

Right, but I mean they
were not men in the service. My hon. friend will correct me if I am wrong, but I understand that this young man's father was an oculist himself.
Yes.

And the application which the young man signed set out the physical requirements for a pilot, but in some way or other he missed that. The file came into the head office and he went on with his training. He was not actually turned down. He was allowed to see if he could qualify. The point in that case was this: I said that if he could qualify, pass our tests and make successful landings without his glasses, he would re-

Supply-National Defence
ceive his certificate. It seemed to me that that was a case in which the young man took that risk when he went into training. If he could make successful landings without glasses, he would ;be granted a certificate. If he could not, then in the interests of the safety of his passengers and for his own safety he should not have a certificate. That was the ground I took. I think the young man took his risk in that respect. He was not turned down because of the fact that he wore glasses, but because he did not pass a test which he must pass without glasses. We have to provide for the case where a man in an accident may lose his glasses and be compelled to land either alone or with passengers without glasses.

I can only speak
from the information I got from the young man and his father. I do not think that at that time it was absolutely necessary that a man should not wear glasses, because certain ones did wear glasses. I do not think he was refused the certificate because he did not make a landing without glasses, because I think he could do so. I do not know that he has ever been given the opportunity.
I think so.

I think not, because just recently I received a letter from him. I am not going to defend the passing of any person with a defect, but I say that this man entered when the restrictions were not so rigid as they became later, and I do not think he knew at the time he entered that wearing glasses would prevent him from getting a certificate. I am absolutely certain of that.

I think my hon. friend
is mistaken as to the regulations. They have always been the same; the restrictions were not made any more rigid after the young man came in. As a matter of fact, as I understand the general regulations, those wearing glasses are not taken, but this was a case where a young man had been allowed to train with glasses, and while we take this extraordinary precaution of saying that a man who wears glasses had better not be allowed to become a pilot at all, we did say in this case that if this young man could make successful landings passed by the officers of the department we saw no reason why a special exception should not be made in his case. My hon. friend may be right in saying that he has never tried to land without glasses, but I am quite positive that I wrote to my hon. friend and told him that the young man would be given the opportunity to pass the test without glasses if he
cared to do so. It is a case perhaps of being over-strict in connection with a matter where we would rather be over-strict than otherwise.

Surely the minister must admit that the requirements with regard to eyesight are much more strict than they were three years ago. I can prove that. Three or four years ago you had not a man who could make the eye tests that they are making to-day. Am I right or wrong in that?

I could not tell my hon.
friend that. All I can say is that the regulations have not changed.

Two or three years ago, when this young man began his training, there were none qualified to make such an examination. Since then you have had men taking a course in the old country, and they can now make the tests. They are extending their experience and teaching others, but at the beginning, three years ago, you did not have a man who could do it. I do not think you had at that time two men in Canada who could make the examination they are making to-day, and I will stand by that.

I speak with the greatest deference in the presence of my hon. friend who, of course, understands thoroughly the service requirements of any man, particularly with regard to, medical qualifications; but I am instructed that my hon. friend is wrong, that we have medical men who had, as my hon. friend had, to do with war service, and who were qualified and so regarded, and that the inspections were made by men who were acknowledged then, and are still, as qualified. My hon. friend is quite right that in this as in any other science we are seeking further information and are endeavouring to perfect it but I would not want to admit either on behalf of the department or of those officers, that they were not qualified to make the examinations.
I should like to know the names of the men who could make those examinations three years ago as they are making them now.
