When agreements have to be made between provinces concerning reciprocity in automobile licenses, or between Canada and the United States concerning tourist travel across the international boundary line, no one would approve of calling in the military staff organization to conduct negotiations. So long as Canadian aviation is left under military control, however, that is exactly what has to be done.
I pass to one other matter, and that is to the cadet services. A number of us have been urging that cadet training is not necessary here in Canada especially under the conditions that now prevail, and further that cadet training is not in the best interests of education itself. We are witnessing at the present time a curious situation under which officials of this government, military officials, are scattering themselves throughout the country and trying to force their military ideas, their unwelcome ideas, upon an unwilling people. For example, one paper in my own city had this to say recently with regard to an outlying suburb, St. James:
Sfc. James school board is to be heartily congratulated on having rejected the blandishments of Colonel Gillespie, representative of the Strathcona Trust when he came to them last week hearing gifts.
Colonel Gillespie wanted the St. James board to introduce cadet training in its schools. The trust, he said, would pay the board $2 per annum per pupil.
Suspecting that the pill would not prove any too palatable, the Winnipeg school board having refused the advances of the Strathcona trust, the colonel proceeded to coat it. The board could, he said, also have folk dances for the girls. But when asked whether the board could have the folk dances without the cadet training he said he did not think so.
Is not this a most peculiar situation, an undignified position for the department to send its officials out trying to coax the various school boards to take up cadet training, and if possible to sugarcoat the pill by suggesting that certain little privileges would be granted to the girls in the school. I quote again:
Unanimously the St. James school board turned down the proposal to allow this wedge of militarism to enter their schools.

What paper is my hon.
friend quoting from?

From a Winnipeg
paper, the Weekly News of the date of Feb-
Supply-National Defence

ruary 8, 1929. The Weekly News is, I am proud to say, a Labour paper. The article goes on:
Five of the St. James school principals were present at the meeting and every one of them advised against the training...
With telling effect councillor Hooper quoted no less an authority than Sir Robert Baden Powell against military training for boys.
I cannot do better than quote Baden Powell's statement:
I find that it has been largely but quite erroneously believed that the boy scout movement is a military one, or at least has militarist tendencies. The mistake is natural, since its figure head holds the rank of general. But it is those who have personally seen something of war who most desire to avert its recurrence on the future generation: it is those who have seen the good and the bad of military training and discipline who can best realize its advantages or disadvantages for educative purposes. Under both these heads I am against using military training for boys. . . .
So much for Baden Powell. Before I close what I have to say on this question of cadet training I should like to quote what may be considered a fair statement of the labour position. Speaking before the Dominion government, when he presented the legislative program of organized labour this year, Mr. Moore, president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, said on the subject of cadet training:
This matter was again under discussion at our last convention, when it was resolved to request that legislation be enacted to provide for the abolition of all money grants for cadet training and other military activites in schools, and that grants be given for the purpose of physical training instead.
We desire to emphasize our beliefs that it is in the best interests of the youth that every encouragement should be given to the development of their physical condition instead of instilling into their minds militaristic ideas by the continuance of the cadet system.
It is our sincere belief that if grants are to be made by the federal government to educational authorities, such grants should be for technical education or purely physical development and not for military training.
What could we do at the present time? We are proposing to spend some $20,000,000 for so-called national defence. There was a resolution on the order paper in the name of my hon. friend from Southeast Grey which I hoped would be discussed, but unfortunately it was not reached. It was the suggestion that for every $100 spent on war preparation, we should spend' $1 in encouraging peace. If we' spend $20,000,000 on war preparation that would mean .that we would spend $200,000 on peace propaganda. Is it too much to ask to spend only $1 on peace for every $100 that is spent on war preparation? Some of us figured out the other day what that $200,000 [Mr. Woodsworth.)
would provide. It would provide a chair for the study of international relationships in every university in Canada. Does that not appeal to the Prime Minister-a chair in international relationships in every university in Canada? Further, it would provide three or four scholarships in every Canadian university for students from other countries who would care to come here and study our Canadian and British institutions. Could we imagine anything that would advertise Canada more widely throughout the world than having a number of foreign students coming to our various universities, spending two or three years here, and then scattering back to their home countries carrying the good wishes of Canada and some knowledge of things -Canadian? On the other hand, that same amount would provide for the sending of three or four students from each university in Canada into different foreign countries to study foreign affairs. To-day we are requiring a certain number of men trained in foreign affairs to be ambassadors, to be -trade representatives, and so on. In the future where are these men to come from? I would hope that thiey would be men of wide esperience, men of special training. I would hope that such positions would be open to all. How are those men to -be trained? I can conceive of no better way than sending some of our brighter -men abroad-
And women.

I beg the pardon
of our one woman member. I can conceive of no better way than sending some of our brightest men and women abroad to study various languages, various cultures, and international affairs, as seen from other angles than our own, and then have them come back to this country. Such students would wonderfully enrich our life, and from them we would be able to pick certain men and women who, as the representatives of this country, would fill official posts abroad in the days to co-me.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we have long recognized' the principle that if we are to have war we must make preparation for war. We have not yet oome to recognize the principle that if we are to have peace we must make some special preparation for peace, and must be -willing to spend something on inculcating peace and training people for a peace program. I say that that $200,000-anyone can figure it out for himself-would -be a sort of glorified international Rhodes scholarship fund, and I can conceive of nothing of which I would be prouder, and that I think would produce a greater moral effect in the world,

Supply-National Defence
than that Canada should take the lead in some such scheme. It would put Canada in the very forefront of the nations. To-day the trouble is that we are feebly copying Europe and the outgrown policies of Europe instead of striking out along our own lines in this new world. We are at a period of great industrial expansion. We all recognize that. The victories of the future will be won not by force of arms, but in the economic and social realms. To-day we are carrying forward the old world traditions, spending our millions on outgrown policies, on policies that can only be inimical to the future welfare of the world. In this young country, so full of the sense of the security, we have the opportunity of adopting some of these new policies which I have had time only to indicate.

When I spoke of flying clubs a little while ago it was with that idea in the back of my mind, to see that civilian clubs automatically carried out these regulations. To me it seems to be necessary for the sound foundation of civil aviation in this country to develop that care and caution and ceaseless attention to these matters of detail, which, if not necessary, it is at least desirable that they should be taught by the influence of discipline and routine.

Our railway engineers and other railway men who are charged with great responsibilities are not under military discipline, and yet they always have their engines in order and are always ready promptly to respond to the call of duty.

That is quite so. But I stated that in my opinion there is no activity where the simple failure to carry out a particular order will lead to such disastrous results as the activity of aviation. There is no doubt about that.
Why should we not conform to the recommendations of the disarmament preparatory commission?

I heard my hon. friend
quote the recommendations of the disarmament preparatory commission, but I think that commission is a long way from having come to any definite conclusion. That commission has -been engaged since 1925 in working out schemes for disarmament -but up to the moment they have not arrived at any conclusions, and they adjourned a short time ago with, I am sorry to say, not too bright prospects of a hopeful outcome of their deliberations for the conference of 1931. I am putting up these considerations against the considerations which my hon. friend has mentioned. Let me deal now with the point he made in regard to civilian aviation, and the statement that such aviation is in itself an incentive to war. He suggested that civilian planes and personnel co-uld be easily adapted to the purposes of war. Now as I mentioned the other day, that is the greatest difficulty which the preparatory commission is finding. This difficulty was expressed by the Spanish represntative before the commission, better, perhaps, than by anyone else. It is found that the nation which has the biggest industrial organization; the nation which -has the biggest transport organization, purely civilian; the nation which has the biggest aircraft organization; the nation which has the biggest and most efficient chemical organization and the best systems of railways and docks and
fMr. Ralston.]
communications; the best system of scientific research; the best agricultural resources-t-he nation which is best- equipped in all these departments of civil life is the nation which can best afford to disarm, for the simple reason that it can arm sooner than any other, using these very resources for military purposes. We cannot ignore the possibility of these resources being used for the -purposes of war. But that, as I w'as trying -to point out to my hon. friend, is far from suggesting that we are adopting these things, or utilising them, or developing our resources chemically, or industrially or agriculturally, or -maintaining our railways for the purpose of war. We are not doing anything of the sort. It is apparent, however, that the nation which is best equipped in all these directions can automatically arm itself soonest for war. And so the representative from Spain-he was dealing with the Russian proposals-expressed the view that general disarmament would result in this, that the nation with the greatest industrial resources would find itself just that much further ahead of -the small nation which was not so equipped; because every nation at the present time has at least a small defence force, and if each nation abandoned its armaments, -and later an- emergency arose, the nation with the small force would' be much slower in bringing its force -back to the status which it held before disarmament.
It is all relative anyway.

Is it not true that the small
nations wanted disarmament? What bearing, then, has my hon. friend's statement on such nations?

I am afraid the question
is based on a false hypothesis. That statement is not correct.
My understanding is that the small nations were disappointed in the attitude of the larger countries.

I do not think my honfriend's hypothesis is correct. Now let me come to another point. Hon. members are right in stating that our geographical position is advantageous. But when they are discussing disarmament, I really do not think they give us credit for the position in which we find ourselves. No nation could be more disarmed than Canada; we have only to compare this country with others in the matter of expenditure. Canada spends $1.59 per head on national defence; the next country is Germany, with $2.60; next comes Russia, with-$3; next, New Zealand, with $3.10; next, South Africa, with $3.19; then even Denmark

Supply-National Defence
with $3.50, and Norway, $3.84. In other words, we spend much less per capita on national defence than any other country in the world.
Another point made by my bon. friend from Southeast Grey is our geographical position. We are fortunate in this, that we have on either side of us a wide ocean so that we have ample warning of any possible aggression. We are in a position where we may prepare for such aggression.
Answering the comment in regard to the size of the force which we maintain, let me remind the committee that the permanent force consists of one man for every three thousand individuals in Canada-not a very large force; it is not even a decent police force. I wish to say here that I do not, nor does the defence department, regard it as a defence force or a standing army in any sense of the word; it is simply an instructional cadre. Our real defence consists in the nonpermanent active militia, which is far from approaching the maximum numerical strength we might maintain on a three year basis, namely, some 240,000 men. Let me give the figures with regard to the militia. In 1914 we had 55,282 men as against 240,000, which would be our possible force, and in 1928, 51,575, or a reduction of nearly 4,000. Take the numbers training. In 1913-14 we gave twelve days' training to 58,563, and in 1928 -disarmament has progressed at least to this extent-we provided twelve days' training for 33,581. In view of these figures, our friends ought to give us credit, in the matter of military expenditures, at least for limiting our activities to a very modest extent, the extent which we are advised is necessary as a minimum.
This brings me to the question asked by my hon. friend: against whom are we preparing? Let me set his mind at rest with regard to the United States. I do not think I can do better than read a statement which was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) not long ago. Speaking at the Assembly of the League of Nations on September 7, 1928, the Prime Minister said:
The Canadian Minister of Finance, in presenting the budget, does not so much as suggest the expenditure of a single dollar through fear of American aggression. Public moneys are saved and utilised for the purposes of productive industry.	,
So that my hon. friends may set their minds at rest on that score.

I had no fear at all
in regard to the United States: I was merely trying to reassure the rest of you.

I am endeavouring to
answer the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

Do I understand
that the standing force exists for the purpose of keeping down any section of our own people who might give trouble?
My hon. friend misunderstands me.

Then it exists in
case of aggression?

I said there was no fear
of aggression from the United States. I am very glad I can assure the committee that I am unable to say against whom we are preparing, and I hope I shall never be able to tell. You might as well ask me to state what burglar will break into my house at night and why there is a policeman on the beat near the flat where I happen to live. It is regarded as part of the national equipment to have a defence force, and our defence force is down to the very minimum-less than a quarter of what it might be. We are maintaining a force which amounts to but one out of every three thousand of the population, and we are training 33,000 men in the camps.
I do not think we could carry disarmament much further, and we are advised that, because of the wide oceans that separate us from other countries, we can reasonably prepare for self defence if that should ever become necessary.
Let me point out to my hon. friend with regard to the covenant of the League of Nations and the Kellogg peace pact, that both these documents expressly provide for selfdefence. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said it was a sort of insinuation against the good faith of other countries to provide a defence force and at the same time sign these documents, but I would point out that the covenant of the League of Nations provides in the first paragraph against resort to war, yet in article 8 it is provided that the members of the league recognize that the maintenance of peace requires the reduction of armaments to the lowest point consistent with national safety, and so on.

But the situation
is different when we all signed.
I do not think there have been any additional signatures.
The United States was brought in by the Kellogg peace pact.

We are not worrying
about the United States, but some other nations are not bound by the terms of these documents. In connection with the Kellogg peace pact let me point out further that whiie it denounces war as an instrument
Supply-National Defence

of national policy, at the same time Mr. Keilogg made an express declaration with regard to self-defence, as follows:
There is nothing in the American draft of an anti-war treaty which restricts or impairs in any way the right of self-defence. That right is inherent in every sovereign state and is implicit in every treaty. Every nation is free at all times and regardless of treaty provisions to defend its territory from attack or invasion and it alone is competent to decide whether circumstances require recourse to war in selfdefence.
Will we not have to abandon the idea of a sovereign state?

I do not understand my hon. friend's question; I am dealing with the point of whether or not a country which provides for self-defence is acting at all contrary to the treaties which have been signed, and I have endeavoured to point out that the convenant of the League of Nations expressly provides for self-defence and that Mr. Kellogg, one of the moving parties in connection with the Briand-Kellogg pact, laid down as a principle that self-defence was always excepted. The question is whether or not we are providing too much in that respect; I have submitted some figures to the house and I think they indicate only a very modest preparation.
I would like to give a few more figures. With regard to the training allotment, for this purpose we spent 11,930,000 in 1913, while in 1928 we spent 81,639,000; in 1922 we had 4.099 men of all ranks in the permanent force, but to-day we have only 3,264, a decrease of over 800; in 1922 the permanent force vote was $6,255,000, while to-day there is only $4,950,000. In discussing this question, which was done by both my hon. friends very fairly and logically, I think they both admitted that there was some necessity for a police force, and my hon. friend from Southeast Grey mentioned that she had no particular objection to retaining the permanent force. Allow me to point out that the permanent force accounts for nearly half this vote of $11,000,000, so at least I feel that I have some support from my hon. friends for these estimates.

How many civilians are
employed and paid out of the permanent force vote?

None; they come under
the civil government vote.
Then I would ask the minister if he would be willing to cut his estimate in half; if so, I will support him.

That is a very sporting
offer, but I cannot accept it. I was endeavouring to point out that the permanent force is only an instructional cadre for the purpose of training the non-permanent active militia.
Did I understand the minister to say that the salaries of civilian employees do not come out of this vote?

There is quite a large
amount in the civil government vote for the pay of civilians, but the actual permanent force vote covers no civilian salaries. I am instructed that 1,671 civilians are employed.

Can the minister state how
much they are paid in a year?
I cannot say exactly, but it might be estimated at $1,500 a year, which is perhaps a low average. That would give a total of about 82,500,000.

I would like to ask the minister if any portion of this item or the items contained in the supplementary estimates, where there is an additional amount of 8250,000 for the Royal Canadian Air Force and $315,000 for civil air operations, provides for the removal of Camp Borden. The minister will recall that early in January a rather large deputation, representing all parts of the county of Simooe and including various county officials, waited upon him and discussed this matter and from time to time there have been references in the press to the possible moving of Camp Borden. When the delegation waited upon the minister the question was fully discussed and many reasons were advanced why no such steps should be taken, and I should like to know now whether any estimate, either main or supplementary, is for that purpose. If there is no such estimate I would like to know if the government has reached any decision with regard to this matter.

Then I am to understand that
the department has reached a definite decision ultimately to abandon Camp Borden and move the equipment to Trenton?

I do not think I can answer that leading question in that way; I can only say that for the present at least both bases will be used, and whether or not Camp Borden will continue to be used will depend upon the needs of the service. I am instructed that for summer training Camp Borden is at least very desirable and that a great deal of use can be made of it, but I cannot say whether or not it will be abandoned ultimately.
The minister does not suggest that there is need for two camps in Canada?

I am instructed that
eventually this might be possible in the summer.

There might be a necessity
for a 'base for hydroplanes which would have to be located near the water.
My information has come from the officers of the department.

If there is any thought of the abandonment of the extensive plant at Camp Borden, I would like to know the reason why. The minister intimates that it may be used, but I gathered from what the minister told the deputation that if Trenton is being selected it is with the intention of the abandonment of Camp Borden. If that is to be the case the house is entitled to know of the tremendous financial sacrifice which would have to be made in that connection. It wouid not be a matter of hundreds of thousands of dollars, it would run into the milions; I think I am quite safe in saying that it would involve a sacrifice of at least $2,500,000 to $3,000,000. If that is the intention I do not want to allow this opportunity to pass without putting upon Hansard some of the figures which the deputation gave to the minister. I suppose the minister has told me all that he feels free to admit, but I can only say that the conclusion I am forced to is that Camp Borden is to be abandoned.

The officers of the department advise that for the next two or three years at least Camp Borden will be needed, and it is possible that that camp may
be needed later, in connection with summer training. As my hon. friend knows, the necessity for a combined sea and land training base makes it very desirable that Trenton should be used. That decision was arrived at after an investigation lasting nearly two years during which over twenty-five different locations were considered by the officers of the department. If my hon. friend desires it, I shall be glad to discuss the financial items with him, but I would say that I have been advised by the officers of the department that it would cost just as much to make Camip Borden a proper base for aviation as it will cost to put Trenton into shape, and we would have the added advantage of a combined base. My hon. friend says that he has figures which show a loss of some millions of dollars, but I do not think that those figures are quite correct. I listened to the discussion which took place when this delegation was here, and I went over the matter very thoroughly with my officers. We came to the conclusion that the expenditures which would be involved in fitting up the base at Trenton would amount to about the same, and I think a little less, than would be required to provide permanent quarters at Camp Borden. We will have the added advantage of the combined base at Trenton and would be overcoming some of the natural difficulties which exist at Camp Borden.

What part of the estimates
have to do with the establishment of the base at Trenton?
None of the main estimates, but the item of $250,000 in the supplementary estimates is to be used for that purpose.

Would the minister give
us some of the points which were considered in selecting Trenton as against other points, say Oshawa or Whitby?

As between Trenton and
Camp Borden?
Oshawa.

No, Whitby; why seleot
Trenton instead of Whitby?

I will look up the
reports. I would suggest that this matter can be fully discussed when we come to the
supplementary estimates.

Mr. Chairman, if there is
one respect more than another in which value results from the vote for national defence, I would say it is from the vote of $2,315,000
Supply-National Defence

for the non-permanent active militia. But in this connection, the minister has stated that the civilians employed in the department were paid $2,500,000, or approximately $200,000 in excess of the total amount appropriated for the non-permanent active militia. It was that militia which made it possible for Canada to recruit 500,000 men during the great war and to send the Canadian corps to France, yet we find that there are civilians employed in the department who cost the country more than is spent upon the non-permanent active militia from one coast to the other. It seems to me that this is a matter which calls for a very careful investigation and1 some readjustments, because every one who served with the Canadian corps realizes that clerical help, such as is being employed in this department at an average of $1,500 per head, could be secured from the permanent force at salaries of approximately one-third of the amount now being paid. In my opinion, anyone who secures a position in the department should be sworn in as a member of the permanent forces of Canada and should be paid according to the rank held.
How about the girls?

The minister knows of his
own personal knowledge that there never was a more efficient body of clerks than those which we had and trained overseas, and the game class of men could be found to-day in the permanent force. It is a shocking thing that the civilians in the department should be paid $200,000 more than is spent upon the whole non-permanent active militia. The officers, men and certain civilians are spending more money on the militia than is the country, and yet we must tell these people who are supporting the militia that while there is no money for them there is plenty of money to employ civilians within the department. Personally, I am very much opposed to this practice and I think an investigation should be carried on to see that everyone employed is sworn in as a member of the forces and not retained as a civilian.

The figures I gave to my hon. friend were a pure guess, and my attention has just been called to the fact that the figure of 1,671 included permanent and1 seasonal employees. For instance we have 429 men who receive $377,900 altogether or something less than $1,000 each.
Those are all civilians?

Yes. Again one would
only have to guess, but the amount is, I think, very much less than that which my hon. friend assumes from the figure.

I am not assuming. My
hon. friend told me it was $2,500,000.

Well, I will accept the responsibility for assuming that. I said $1,500, just averaging the salaries. I thought they were all full-time employees. The only way to deal with the matter would' be to make up an exact statement. If my hon. friend wants another estimate I might suggest $1,000 as liberal which would mean $1,671,000. I agree absolutely with my hon. friend as to the contribution which is made by the non-commissioned officers and men to the non-permanent active militia. Two years ago I gave figures showing that in nearly 50 per cent of the units either the whole or a portion of the pay is pooled by officers or men or both, *this showing a pretty generous contribution to the non-permanent active militia, but my hon. friend will admit that all these other votes for contingencies, engineer services and works, general stores, manufacturing establishments, topographic survey and transport and freight are partly non-permanent active militia and partly permanent force, and very much more for the former than for the latter. So in estimating the amount expended on the non-perimanent active militia, one would have to consider the payments under these items as well as the actual non-permanent active militia vote, which really represents only pay and allowances together with expenses in connection with training.

Mr. Speaker, I have read the evidence in this case, which seems to me to be one that is somewhat extraordinary in character. It involves, I think, an altogether new principle. It has been said time and again in this bouse that the only ground upon which the senate committee grants a divorce is adultery, which has been called the statutory ground. As a matter of fact, as has been previously pointed out, there is no statute defining the grounds upon which divorce is granted by this parliament. There is no law whatever governing the question. In a case like this, or in any other divorce case, I contend that there i3 first the general principle of divorce and, secondly, the special cause for which the divorce is granted in the particular bill. Now if, as claimed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), this divorce is not granted for the cause supposedly admitted to be the only one for which divorce is granted, then a new aspect of the matter presents itself. In this instance, if, as claimed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the evidence establishes not adultery but desertion, then we are granting the divorce for a cause other than that generally alleged to be the only one for which this parliament grants divorce; and it seems to me that this aspect of the case must be examined before the bill passes. There is the general principle governing all these bills, and there is the particular principle on which the divorce is granted in the bill before the committee. Suppose, for example, a divorce bill came before us based upon the assertion that the petitioner had been insulted by his or her consort; then it would mean that we should be granting a divorce on an entirely different ground. It seems to me, therefore, that on the second reading of any bill the house must consider the basis on which the divorce is granted.
So far as the evidence in this case is concerned, I have not read it sufficiently to form a decided opinion upon it. Mr. Chairman, I am
more opposed to this vote than to any other under the heading of national defence; I think it is the most vicious of all. I am very sorry that it always comes up at the end of the session when hon. members are tired and certainly do not want to hear a speech on the subject, but I feel impelled to make a few remarks once again in connection with this matter. I wish more members of the house would take an interest in this matter and I can promise that if someone else would speak on cadet training I would refrain from doing so.
I believe that cadet training is military and not physical training, as is often claimed by the Department of National Defence. In physical training the health of the individual being trained is the central idea, while in cadet training the protection of the state is the central idea, so that these two are quite different and should not be confused. I think we may conclude that cadet training is military training. Each cadet instructor holding a certificate from the department and possessing the necessary qualification receives an annual grant of $2 per cadet. If I am incorrectly informed I should be glad to have the minister correct me.
Up to a certain number.

Up to fifty cadets, and he receives SI per cadet in excess of that

number. This being the case, we can be sure that if the instructor has a bias on the subject at all it will be in favour of cadet training and the tendency will be for all the teachers who are cadet instructors to go in for cadet training. In addition to this, in the province of Ontario the Department of Education makes a grant of $50 to each school board having an organized cadet corps of not less than 20 cadets.
There came to my hand recently the 1929 year book of the Glebe Collegiate Institute, on page 29 of which I find the following:
The annual cadet dance of the 94th and 1070th cadet corps was held at the Glebe gymnasium on May 18th. The dance was a colorful event with the brilliant uniforms of our guests from the different military units of the city.
So that is at least one use for the permanent force; they supplied the colour at the cadet dance. There is a very close connection between the military units and the cadet corps. The minister cannot claim that the number of cadets has not increased. This afternoon he claimed that the department is not as military as it was some years ago, but the figures with reference to cadets show a rapid and steady increase. In the year 1909 the number of cadets in Canada was 9,000-again, if I am wrong, I shall be ,tlad to be corrected -and the total expenditure for that year is not recorded. In 1914, the year of the outbreak of the war, the number was 47,000 and the cost amounted to $392,000; the year after the war closed, 1919-20, the number of cadets had jumped to 65,000, and the cost had amounted to $374,000; last year, 1927-28, the cadets had increased to 130,000 and the cost-
Hear, hear.

The applause shows
more of the old-time patriotism rather than good sense. The cost had increased to $500,000. According to the statistics of 1926, the number of cadets in Great Britain and northern Ireland wias only 34,156, as compared to 112,463 in Canada for the same year. To put it in another way, the province of Ontario had only 1,000 less cadets than Great Britain and northern Ireland. According to the 1921 census, the population of Great Britain was 42,767,530, while the population of Canada in the same year was 8,788,481. If that is patriotism, which I doubt very much, then we are much more patriotic than is the mother country.
In the past war has been glorified, not only in Canada but throughout the world. It had to be glorified to keep it going, because it was a business which necessitated the killing

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
of a lot of people; it caused tremendous misery, and unless some sort of halo was thrown around it, it could never have gone on as long as it has. The schools have been used as the medium for this glorification of war, but public opinion throughout the world has changed and they have denounced and claim to have renounced war. How can we expect to evolve new and peaceful means of settling international disputes and expect them to succeed if we do not give the youth of our country new ideals. Do we expect that these things will come of themselves? Do we think that peace requires no effort, no expenditure and no organization? Apparently the government does, although I know that some of the individuals composing the government do not. However, judging from their actions as a government I can only conclude that they think that peace is a thing which will come of its own volition and is not something which has to be worked for.
Supposing we did not use the schools to bring forth these new ideals, but left the youth of the country free to think the thing out for themselves, then we would be on fairly safe ground. But we do not do that; we superimpose upon the youth ideas which have proved to be worthless and we use the military department to do that at a cost of half a million dollars per year. I think-perhaps I had better not say that; I will go on.
Say it.

The very fact that we have military training in our schools causes the boys who take the training, as well as the girls who do not, to think of war as the one and only means of settling international' disputes. They have not been taught any other means of settlement, and so they think that the means which they have been taught is the one to take. As Lord Roberts said: The possession of an art stimulates the wish to practise that art; it is the law of human nature.
The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), speaking in the Kellogg pact debate, quoted Shakespeare as follows: The sight of means to do ill deeds makes deeds i'll done.
Both those sayings are very true and they certainly apply to this case. When difficulties arise the student who has been military trained naturally thinks of brute force as the one and only method of settling disputes and does not think of calling upon the resources of the mind and spirit as a means of settlement. In other words, his mind is biased 78594-205i
on the subject and he is prevented from reaching higher ground by the very ideas we have superimposed upon him.
I do not think that anyone will deny that teachings in the schools can change the thoughts of a people on any subject in little more than a generation. We have some remarkable examples of that. The military teaching in the schools of Germany changed that country from a peaceful to a military one. The glorifying of commerce in the schools of Japan made that country a great commercial country within a very short time. Through their teaching of goodwill and the spirit of fellowship and brotherhood, the schools of Denmark within a generation made that country one of the outstanding countries in cooperation and peace. I think our schools should be used to develop the idea that no 6ne can be an efficient citizen who has not an international outlook. Our schools should seek to develop the international mind, and we should try to get away from the old days when it was thought: "They should take who have the power, and they should keep who can." That is not so universally the spirit to-day as it was a few years ago. We do not so firmly believe that the race is to the swift and the battle to the strong; we are emerging from a competitive age into a cooperative age. I do not think I need to point out the trends because I am addressing intelligent people who have noted them here and there. To my mind the schools at least should be left free to give the lead on this great subject of reaching higher moral ground; in showing the people that after all the world is a community in which we all live, and that the good of one is the good of all. This afternoon I quoted the right hon. the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition to show that they thought that we had left the old methods behind and were taking up new ways of settling international disputes, and I will not repeat the quotations.
Those who support military training for the youth of this country say that it is a splendid means of instilling discipline. I think it was Brigadier-General MacBrien or Major-General MacBrien-I would not get the titles mixed for anything in the world, as I do not want to take any glory away from him-who, speaking in Montreal on this subject, took great trouble to point out the benefit of the discipline that came through cadet training. I think those who make that claim confuse self-control with regimentation. There is a great difference between discipline as an aid to education and education as an aid to disciplined manhood and womanhood.

The one is force; the other is character. I believe that a cadet is trained not to order his own affairs, but to be an efficient instrument in the hands of his superiors, doing the things that they command for the purposes they desire.
Another great argument that is advanced in favour of cadet training and keeping everybody ready for a world scrap all the time is that, with human nature as it is, we need always to be prepared, going on the assumption that human nature is a very low thing and that it never changes. I was interested in reading what Tagore, the great Indian poet, had to say on this subject. Hon. members will have noticed that Tagore visited Canada, and while he was in the city of Vancouver he addressed the International Educational Conference there. He has this to say about human nature:
In prehistoric age man ate man. Any claiming it an anti-social or immoral practice would be told it was human nature, but human instinct of cannibalism changed its physical character and took an economic aspect. I know the spirit of fight is ingrained in man, but the urging is also inherent in him to transmute its nature from the brutal to the human. When he has passed through his present state of physical ferocity he will, no doubt, have more than enough to fight about, but on a higher plane, intellectual, moral and spiritual.
I think human nature does change and I do not think the argument that has been advanced is any argument in favour of cadet training.
But probably the strongest argument against it is that it is contrary to the true spirit of education. The purpose of education is to develop the full rounded powers of the individual, to develop initiative, the power of selection of action, the will to act. Education should enlarge the vision of the student and prepare him to live in an ever-widening community.
Could we have a little more order?

It is quite time there were more women in the House of Commons. Women consider the things that affect boys and girls as being of very great importance. Men are too prone to think that only things that concern dollars and cents are important. In any worthwhile educational system the child and the interests of the child, and not the state and the interests of the state, should be the centre. In true education the child would be the centre of interest and everything would revolve around that idea. This would in the long run be better for the state.
''Miss Macphail.]
Military training subordinates the will of the individual, and that certainly is contrary to true education. It kills initiative. An old poem, familiar to us all, describes very aptly what it does:
Their's not to reason why,
Their's but to do and die.
There is no selection for the individual and he becomes a machine. I think I put on Hansard three or four years ago a quotation from Bertrand Russell on the Principles of Social Reconstruction. Let me quote three or four lines from John Langdon Daines, a well known English educator. He says:
The result-
Of cadet training, to which he is very much opposed.
-is that the young generation has no chance of having free ideals and shaping evolution by their means; instead he is shaped to the existing forms and to the ideas which it pleases his rulers he should possess.
In this case the House of Commons are his rulers. John Dewey, who is very well known in Canada as a distinguished American educator, has this to say about military training:
Military training "is undemocratic, barbaric and educationally wholly unwise."
We are coming to the time when we shall be scientific enough to take the advice of people who are experts on any given subject. These men whom I have quoted are experts in the field of education and we should listen to them.
Recently a survey was made of the school system of British Columbia by two educational experts, Doctor Putman and Doctor George Weir of the University of Columbia. They had this to say about military training in the schools:
We take strong exception to the plan of having any part of this work done by militia officers, who naturally give it a military bent.
But as the Minister of National Defence pointed out to me last year, a second commission was appointed and it gave a contrary opinion. Whether that was because the first one did not give an opinion suitable to the powers that be, I do not know. It looks as if it were the reason and I would need to know some of the facts of the case before I would believe it was not. This year many people went to the educational conference in Vancouver, the one that was addressed by Tagore and also by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. What was said there on cadet training, I do not know, but something must have been said about it, because the result of it was that the Lethbridge Board of Education decided,

after one of their number had attended that conference, that they would no longer have cadet training in the schools of Lethbridge and they discontinued it. The organized farmers in the different provinces of Canada have again and again taken their stand as being opposed to cadet training. Organized labour has done the same thing many times. Certain women's organizations have taken a similar stand. None of the churches has yet reached that point, but they are getting there. The question has been discussed and a motion to the effect was almost carried last year. There is still hope that some time before long they, too, will take a stand against military training in schools. The most forward-looking women's organization on peace that I know of is the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom, whose international president is Jane Addams of Hull House, Chicago. These are outstanding women who have given a good deal of time and thought, and indeed much suffering, in the cause of peace. At their Dublin conference, which I unfortunately was not able to attend, they passed' the following resolution:
We women of the Women's International League are of the opinion that the time has come to educate all children for peace; we hold it to be a crime against the souls of ripening youth to picture war to them as a necessity, or even as a moral duty; to train them in war-handicraft and instruct them in the art of killing.
I think that is very beautifully put, and it is all very true.
In conclusion, let me say that I am opposed to cadet training in schools because I believe it is contrary to true education, making the state, and not the child, the first consideration. I am oipposed to it because I believe it is not good physical training, because it cramps the mind and lowers the moral sense of youth, causing it to rely upon force rather than upon character. It does not result in self-discipline, and it prevents active and understanding work as a world citizen, as the word is constituted now. It discounts faith and counts on fear. It is contrary to the teachings of great moral and religious teachers of the ages.
To teach military training and the spirit of peace at the same time is to brand ourselves as moral cowards and hypocrites in the eyes of youth, and I know nothing we could do that would be more disastrous for this country and the world at large. I therefore move, seconded by the bon. member for Battle River, that item No. 72 be reduced by $499,999.

I should like to review in a few sentences the history of this movement.
Ever since 1862 provision has been made in Canada for cadet training in the schools. Between 1908 and 1910 agreements were entered into between the different provinces under which the provinces that desired physical training and cadet training might have it, and might have grants accordingly. Every province has come into the scheme. The scheme is purely optional. There is no compulsion about it of any kind or description; any school at any time which does not desire it need not have it, and any boy whose parents do not want him to take cadet training does not need to take it.
The appropriation of physical training as compared with cadet training is indicated by these figures: last year there were trained for physical training certificates 6,644 teachers, all at the expense of the country, as against only 318 who trained as cadet instructors.
I have given the syllabus to the committee on former occasions. It includes physical training, squad drill, signalling, the teaching of alertness, preparation for vocations, first aid, scouting, rifle shooting, organized games, lectures on citizenship and lectures by business men and others on various vocations. Those are the general subjects which are taken up in connection with cadet training purely, but physical training constitutes the greatest proportion of the cadet training as carried on in the schools at the present time.
I think the best and shortest answer which might be made is that by far the greatest number of institutions in respect to which the grant is made are in the province of Quebec, that the greatest increase this year by far in cadet training has been in the province of Quebec, that the movement is supported by the clergymen of the province of Quebec, who obviously cannot be charged with a desire to cultivate the militaristic spirit. I do submit, as I have submitted to this committee before, that the amendment should not carry.

I cannot let the last words of the Minister of National Defence pass without giving some explanation. His words would leave the impression that generally in the province of Quebec the clergy or the educational institutions are in favour of cadet training. They are not, if the minister will allow me; for I know the province of Quebec a little better than he does. Unfortunately, I admit, some of the educational institutions have been induced to adopt this system, and I mu9t say that some of them have adopted it not from high patriotic motives but simply because of the money grants; and I am not especially proud of

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
them for that, nor do I think that a very large proportion of the citizens of the province of Quebec are especially proud of them for it.
The number of people in the province of Quebec, as elsewhere, who agree with the general principles that have just been expressed by the hon. menfber for Southeast Grey is much larger than the minister may imagine; but in the province of Quebec as elsewhere there are people who will let themselves go for a long time before they realize the consequences of their action.
The minister says that this movement has been in operation for sixty years. Of course, a good many things have been in operation for sixty years and over. Many things were in operation before the war that led the world to the war. It was because many things were let go for years before the war that the war suddenly caught the world without its realizing what was upon it. Of course, a few men did realize what was coming and a few men took advantage of that blindness of the world at large to prepare for the war and launch it upon the world. But since the war, some of these men even have come to see things differently. There were men in various countries of the world who before the war were preparing both young and older men for war, but who are now endeavouring to prepare them for peace. That is precisely the question. Are we going to do after the war the things that will counteract the forces for war, just as before the war we did the things that prepared for and led to the war?
We send every year a delegate or several delegates to the League of Nations, and we have adhered to every public peace move. Splendid orations have been made by the official representatives of Canada at Geneva and elsewhere to show that Canada is prepared to do everything for the cause of peace. But the cause of peace or any other cause is not advanced simply by speeches. It is advanced by the general trend of public opinion. It is advanced by such moral and political forces as are brought to bear upon public opinion to lead it in the right direction.
If we start with the schools, it is not only the question of cadet training in itself, but it is the whole tendency of education in the schools. It varies according to the provinces and according to the educational institutions; but certainly there are some educational institutions in this country which are still going on as they did before the war, developing in the minds of the children something unnatural which changes the nature of the child, and that is the idea that war and everything connected with war is the most glorious thing for the nation and for the individuals com-

posing the nation. The child goes out from the school with that notion, that the great heroes of history are not those men and women who work for peace or for moral or intellectual progress, but those men who are forceful enough or brutal enough to be great conquerors and victors by force of arms. The heroes of all history are the war heroes. Take most of the textbooks still used in our schools in all the provinces, in Quebec and elsewhere. In the books used in Ontario you will see more names of English officers and generals, and in Quebec more names of French generals before the conquest, but through them all runs the same spirit, that war is the most glorious thing which the nation or the individuals composing it can think of. I admit that this government and this parliament have nothing to do with that part of education, but when you take all these things together, the encouragement given by this government to cadet training, glorifying military heroes in the school textbooks and the general trend given to the child's mind in the schools all over the country, it simply means this, that while we talk peace in public speeches and at international gatherings we are not doing the main thing to prepare the future generations in this country for peace. They are doing more of that in the old countries. They are doing it at present in Germany, in France, also, and, of course, in England, and it is being done not only by individuals but by institutions. They are developing the peace mind, and they are not being discouraged by the public powers. That is especially true of Germany. Whatever view may be taken of the responsibility of Germany in the great war, and probably Germany was chastised by defeat, if there is a country in Europe at the present time which is working for peace in that most efficient manner which is so characteristic of the Germans it is Germany. They have gone to the root of the thing. In the years that preceded the war, and more particularly before the war of 1870, the schools of Germany were said to be preparatory schools for the army. Today the schools of Germany, from the primary school to the university, are the preparatory schools of the peaceful generations to come. Having felt the scourge of war, having realized that war is not only a crime against humanity, but the greatest calamity that can befall any nation, they are now preparing the youth of their country to prevent war in the future. They are not doing it to the same extent in France unfortunately, but there also, there is at least a certain reaction against war. In England the reaction is stronger, and I hope

with the political change on the horizon that the work of peace will be enhanced there as well as in Germany.
Well now, what are we going to do, first, as a portion of the British Empire, and second, as one of the nations of the world? Are we going to stand pat? Are we going to proceed along the old routine, which has been followed since 1862 the minister has just said; or are we going to react energetically and intelligently? Are we going to make our professions of love of peace true or not; or, as the member for Southeast Grey has said, are we going to stamp ourselves, not intentionally but as a matter of fact, with the stamp of hypocrisy by preaching peace before the world and not putting it into practice at home?
The great difficulty in Geneva to-day is to prepare the nations for disarmament. Everybody admits that it is useless to talk of peace if the nations do not disarm. Why does not the cause of disarmament make more progress? Because some of the nations connected with the League of Nations have not disarmed according to the solemn pledge they gave in the Versailles treaty, on the pretence that under present conditions they cannot disarm. The result is that no nation disarms.
Physical disarmament is of course very important. It is very essential and very practical to reduce the extent and the effectiveness of the weapons of war. But it is still more important to disarm morally, it is still more important to change the mind which produces the causes which finally make use of the arms of war. Warships, cannons, poison gases do not start by themselves, they do not create the causes of war. They are more or less powerful means of war in the hands of the government of any country. But they create the scourge of war the moment the moral causes of war crop up or create the occasion which launches war. The physical means are simply the means to the end, and physical disarmament will not be accomplished, or will be useless, until moral disarmament has been brought about.
Now', can we educate the youth of Germany, or the youth of France, or the youth of England, or of Italy in the love of peace? No, we cannot. But we can do something to educate the children of Canada in the love of peace. Does this government think it is a duty to the Canadian nation to give the various provinces money in order to prepare cannon fodder in the form of young boys taught at school to love war, to love military uniforms, to love the glamour of war until they have tasted of it? If we are sincere in our love of peace why do not we make some offers to the various provinces to help them in establishing
some kind of peace education? I am sure that in the province of Quebec some of those institutions to which the minister has referred would be mighty glad to organize a peace department rather than a war department; but they are still doing what the minister says the federal government has been doing-they continue to do what they did before. Well, they should be induced to do something else.
This afternoon I have been reading an extremely interesting lecture given in Paris -and this is a sign of the times-by a Hungarian diplomat, one of the representatives of his country at the League of Nations. Of course, four or five years ago he would not have been listened to in Paris. Discarding his official capacity, and speaking as a human being appealing to his fellow beings, whether of French or of foreign origin, he asked them and I ask now: Why don't we look through this question? If we do, then we find out that there are two or three obstacles to the establishment of peace. One of them, of course, i3 the absurd system of treaties that was built up in the days of rancour and hatred immediately after the war, built up by the victors against the vanquished, which naturally could not be a sensible peace. But that may be arranged, and of course will be arranged. Common sense will prevail over blind passion. The second obstacle is the system of alliances which arose out of those nonsensical treaties. That also may be arranged. But those two causes will not disappear before you have created in the masses of the people of each country a state of mind which will not only permit but impose such a reform. Disarmament will not be brought about in every country the world over, treaties will not be revised, alliances will not be broken and replaced by the real exercise of the forces of arbitration under the League of Nations, until in all countries that peace spirit is created.
Well, that peace spirit will not grow of itself. We have helped to create the contrary spirit. For generations we have been doing that without realizing the import of our action. Governments were no more realizing what they were coming to than those educational institutions in Quebec or elsewhere are realizing to-day what they are preparing for the next generation. For years they have received a certain amount of money from the federal government to costume a few boys, making them caricatures of soldiers, and they continue doing that. Well, suppose we assisted practically and do something to counteract that spirit, to prepare armies of peace, and to develop the mind of peace in those boys in-

stead of the mind of war. The mind of war develops by itself under that false system. Then with a certain degree of pride and sincerity we could go ito Geneva and elsewhere and prove that within the British Empire, as one of the main units of that splendid galaxy of nations, we are helping the cause of peace, the cause of disarmament, and that through the British Empire as well as through our own individual influence at Geneva and elsewhere we are also helping the cause of peace.
So long as we do not take the means to cure, the war spirit within ourselves it is almost useless to talk peace outside. It is not altogether useless to do so, because it enables a few people to realize, as the member for southeast Grey realized long ago, and has so expressed it, that there is something false in this system. But this government which is pledged to peace, this government which in the province of Quebec especiaily has appealed to all the feelings of peace against the warlike party on the other side of the house, should be consistent in Quebec and elsewhere, and advocate a peace policy not only at election time when their candidates appeal to that feeling in Quebec, but in this parliament and in all the provinces of the Dominion.

There were 199 students at the college last year, and the full vote of $375,000 was spent.

I would like the minister to tell the committee as to the real value of the Royal Military College, because I believe there is not an institution in Canada to-day that is doing such a splendid work. You will find there students from the various high schools throughout Canada. They have gone there in doubt as to their future, and they have come out fortified with knowledge and vision, with character beyond words, and they take a prominent place among the bright young men of Canada. I visited the Royal Military College some weeks ago and I found there students from every part of Canada, including western British Columbia, and among them students that I myself had taught in Prince Rupert. I would ask the minister to stand up right now and let us know why he is not adding to this vote, and why he is a little bit timid about showing the educational value of the Royal Military College and asking for only $375,000.
What was the number of students who attended the institution in 1920, and what was the cost that year?
I am sorry I cannot give my hon. friend the number of students, but I have here the number of graduates. There were 33 in 1920, and 34 last year. The amount voted in 1920-1921 was $349,819.
What is the basis of admission to the college, and do the students pay any of their expenses themselves? I notice that the cost per student figures out to about $1,900.

First they pay $100 a year, and then for the four years they pay in addition $1,050 for clothing, and so forth; so that the four-year course costs them $1,450. The method of admission is by selection according to merit. My hon. friend will remember the discussion in the house last year. The word "merit" was retained in the statute, and I can assure him that that has been the basis of admission. Allotment is made to the various provinces according to population and applications are received, the educational qualifications being the matriculation examination for the province. There are certain regulations with regard to the age limit and regulations particularly with regard to physical fitness. Having regard to the marks made, showing the scholastic 
ability of the student, together with his age and physical fitness, selection is made by a selection board up to the allotment of each province.
I am pleased that the minister has given us the qualifications for entrance to the college. For the students from British Columbia, for example, is the senior or junior matriculation essential?
Without looking up the regulations, I do not think that senior matriculation is required, although senior matriculation gives the student just that much better standing and a preference in selection.

I do feel that the Minister
of National Defence has not yet realized the wonderful work that this institution is doing for the youth of Canada. I do say from my knowledge of that institution, and of the young men who were trained there and have come forth from that institution with courage and faith and knowledge and vision, that the minister should stand up to-night and ask not merely for $375,000, but for a larger vote. He should go further; he should encourage in every possible way our Canadian youth to enter an institution wherein virility, purity of life and courage towards attainment are developed to the limit. I do think, sir, that the Canadian people should be proud of the Royal Military College at Kingston and I am glad to be able to say to-night from honest conviction that it is one of the finest institutions in the whole Dominion for educating the young ambitious youth of Canada.

Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, it is not worth the trouble for me to say that I do not agree with our very affable and polished Irish colleague, but I cannot let his remarks pass without protest. If we want to instil courage in our young men let us elect them to the House of Commons; that will develop it if anything will.
No.

Yes, it will-if they
are men. I think the cost of training our youth at the military college is excessive. It is usually people well able to afford the cost of education who send their children to the military college, and the $1,400 paid by the students for four years is certainly not much.

It is not much for four years. But my main objection is not to the cost. As I have said very many times in this

Supply*-National Dejence
house, we have two schools of thought in Canada; one which thinks security can come by peaceful means, and the other which thinks it can come only by military preparation. The military college was established in the days when the latter school of thought was more dominant than it is to-day-for it is still more or less dominant. In those days the blue* blooded young men were sent there. By the way, I do not know how they became blue-blooded; I thought that all Canadians were "red-blooded" anyway. The colour of the blood is a bit confusing anyway. Some of the so-called "cream" of Canada went to the Royal Military College, the idea being that it was a little more exclusive than most educational institutions and that those young men might serve as officers in the Canadian militia in the event of war.
The reason I object to the grant to this college is that the Dominion government is backing the one school of thought in Canada, the military school, and is giving absolutely no help to the other school of thought, which as I said before, think that security does not come from warlike methods. It is high time that we scrapped the military college at Kingston. If the blue-blooded people of Canada-my blood is red-want to train their sons in military tactics, they have already by special legislation taken enough money from the common people to enable them to build a college for the purpose. I cannot sit silent while the House of Commons votes money for the Royal Military College. My own opinion is that it develops snobbery. If it is not military it is snobbish; I think it is possibly both. The young men can go to any university in Canada and be educated for civil life. But, Mr. Chairman, I am getting into deeper water all the time; not only do I disagree with my friend the Minister of National Defence, but now I find myself out of sympathy with the very affable member for Skeena (Mr. Brady).

It is not often, Mr. Chairman, that I really feel at home in the House of Commons, but I do now after listening to the very genial and lovable member for Southeast Grey, who has endeared herself not only to the government-which she often supports-but to the official opposition which she likewise supports, for not later than yesterday evening she supported us on one of the most vital questions that has come before the House of Commons this session. I refer to the debate on the Australian treaty. But much as I revere and appreciate her opinions,-words to me are very significant,-to-night she used three outstanding words when speaking of the Royal Military College - "fashionable" - "blue-blooded" - "snobbery". Now, candidly, I should like to accompany the hon. member for Southeast Grey to the Royal Military College at Kingston, to disprove her statements. During three years only on two occasions has it been my privilege to speak in reply to the very charming and very lovable member for Southeast Grey. After all, hon. members will realize that in the days "when knighthood was in flower" and heroes set out in quest of adventure to rescue some charming female in distress, valour and sentiment were supported by good judgment and discretion. Therefore when to-night I heard the hon. member for Southeast Grey say that the Royal Military College was only for those who are " fashionable," " blue-blooded" and "snobbish", I realized, for the first time in three years that the charming member for Southeast Grey had not visited that splendid institution known as the Royal Military College. Now, I know something of the young men who are educated in the Royal Military College at Kingston. While I would be the last man in the world to reflect upon the integrity, sincerity and truthfulness of the hon. member for Southeast Grey, I must tell her that I know thoroughly the type of young men who go through the Royal Military College at Kingston. The hon. and charming member I know has read her history, and she must know something of the days of the plebeians in ancient Rome. Perhaps there is an analogy between the plebeian and the modern democrat, but I wish to tell the hon. member for Southeast Grey right now, that in my sixteen years knowledge of the Royal Military College not one of the students from British Columbia was fashionable, blue-blooded or snobbish-not one. Who were they Mr. Chairman? They were the young boys who failed to get the benefit of the higher education that the universities afford; they were trying to find their way; they were boys who needed the discipline which the Royal Military College could give in order that they might find their feet. And they found what they sought. I wish to say right now, in the presence of the hon. and gracious member for Southeast Grey, that the young men trained in the Royal Military College in Kingston have come forth from that institution not merely as scientific men-and I know many of them who have taken their B.Sc. and M-Sc.-but as an honour to their fathers and mothers, and they are the pride of the community in which they live. Everyone knows the persuasive powers in this

house of the hon. member for Southeast Grey. The moment she rises to her feet, silence reigns in the house, and all give her obeisance. No matter what she says, the male sex bows to her judgment as it has ever done in all ages, to the devobo femineo sexu. Therefore I say that no matter what the hon. member for Southeast Grey says, whether she condemns the Royal Military College or whether she opposes the vote provided for the national defence of Canada, we realize that at least her heart is with us, because I have never yet found myself disagreeing with her even though at times, tentatively, she tries to tell us that if we, the Conservative party, are not good she will vote with the government in power, which she seldom does.

The airport at Montreal
was established as part of an imperial air route, having regard to the suggestion made at the 1926 imperial conference for the development, if possible, of dirigible communication between Great Britain and the continent of North America. At that time the Prime Minister, who was representing Canada at the conference, undertook that provision should be made for a mooring mast and necessary terminal facilities in Canada, and the aerodrome at St. Hubert was purchased and equipped with that object in view. Perhaps my hon. friend does not know that any commercial companies who are using that aerodrome are paying for the use of it; it is not free.

I raise now the claim of a
city like Vancouver; it appears to me that there is a strong claim for the province of British Columbia. During a great part of the year we are five nights on the train from the city of Ottawa-five nights to communicate between the capital of the country and such a city as Vancouver, and six nights so far as Victoria is concerned. We have a strong claim for the establishment of an air service between that part of the country and central Canada; indeed, our claim is stronger than that of Montreal. I appreciate the fact that Montreal has a strong claim, and also the fact that the establishment of the aerodrome there is partly the result of the imperial conference.
Altogether.

If that was the sole reason- the request of the imperial government-this country would not be spending the money which it is spending on that port. The fact is that this country recognizes its responsibility in developing its airways; that work must be done. Therefore I now advance the

Practically none of the increase will be devoted to new equipment; the greater part will be devoted to the development of air routes.

I should like to take this opportunity to point out that economy certainly should not be practised in regard to equipment. An aeroplane engine is not a very costly piece of mechanism; I suppose $20,000 or $30,000 would pay for the ordinary engine, and I think we should realize that human lives are constantly depending upon these machines.
My hon. friend is under a misapprehension; the cost of an ordinary engine is from $4,000 to $8,000.

Then that makes my argument much stronger, although of course some engines cost much more than that. Wherever else we economize we should not do so in connection with the equipment of our air service. During my casual visit I was very much impressed with the type of Canadian manning our air service, not only as to personal character but as to the spirit manifested; it seems to me that a new tradition is being created which some day will rival the tradition of the sea. Could the minister tell us what assistance, if any, is given by his department to the different cities in the establishment of airports?

I outlined to the committee a few moments ago the assistance we give. We have nothing to do directly with the purchase, the la3ung out or the preparation of the airports. Our assistance consists of two things; first, we provide the services of officers of the department as frequently as they are necessary, to make surveys of the proposed airports and to advise as to their suitability or as to what is necessary to make them suitable. Is it a fact that the government presents two airplanes to any city which inaugurates a flying club?
That is a fact.
Under what conditions is that presentation made?

The conditions are contained in an agreement, and I will give my hon. friend a brief resume. The club must have at least ten men who have qualified as pilots, either in the war or by other training; the club must agree to provide an instructor and pay for his services, and provide for the maintenance of the machines and a suitable place for operation. If that, is done an agreement is entered into and the department supplies two planes. A bond is taken to provide against injury to the planes through breach of the regulations or on account of negligence. A further provision is contained in the agreement whereby $100 is paid to the club for every man who passes as a certified pilot as a 
result of the activities of the club. A further provision is that if within one year the club provides another plane, then the department will provide one also.
